message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Specialized for parallel, data‑intensive tasks – originally for rendering graphics, now also used for scientific computing, machine learning, etc. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32), each highly optimized for low latency, complex control flow, and large caches. | Hundreds or thousands of simpler cores, optimized for high throughput on many identical operations. |
| **Instruction Set** | Complex instruction set (CISC) with sophisticated branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution, and large cache hierarchies. | Simpler instruction set (often SIMD) focused on executing the same operation across many data elements simultaneously. |
| **Memory Hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, deep memory hierarchy, low latency access. | Smaller per‑core caches; relies on massive bandwidth from shared memory pools. |
| **Typical Workloads** | Single‑threaded or lightly parallel tasks, branching logic, I/O, OS services. | Data‑parallel tasks like matrix multiplication, image processing, neural network inference/training, physics simulations. |
| **Performance Metrics** | Measured in instructions per cycle (IPC), clock speed, single‑thread performance. | Measured in floating‑point operations per second (FLOPS), memory bandwidth, throughput. |
| **Energy Efficiency** | Optimized for low power per core, but overall power can be high due to many cores. | Very efficient at high throughput per watt for parallel workloads. |
| **Programming Model** | Traditional imperative programming, multi‑threading, OS scheduling. | Parallel programming models (CUDA, OpenCL, Vulkan compute, DirectCompute, Metal, etc.). |

In short, a CPU excels at handling diverse, sequential tasks with low latency, while a GPU shines when you need to perform the same operation on a huge amount of data in parallel. Modern systems often combine both: the CPU manages overall system control and complex logic, while the GPU accelerates heavy numerical or graphical workloads.
